data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["Biological natural selection has no conscious agent making a 'preference,' whereas scientists do","Survival in nature often correlates with future reproductive success (inductive link), whereas Popper denies this correlation for theories","Evolutionary fitness is defined by actual future reproduction, while corroboration is strictly historical"],"overturn_conditions":["If it can be shown that 'severity' of a test implicitly relies on an inductive assumption that nature behaves uniformly.","If acting on a theory for practical purposes (e.g., building a bridge) necessarily implies believing it will hold, which equates to assigning it high probability."],"shared_structure":["Selection based on past survival rather than predicted future frequency","Goal is error elimination rather than truth accumulation","Status is provisional and non-probabilistic"],"source_memory_refs":["Popper_Conjectures_Refutations_Ch10","Popper_Logical_Scientific_Discovery_Sec79"],"transfer_claims":["Just as we study the fittest organism to understand adaptation limits, not to guarantee its offspring's survival, we adopt the best-corroborated theory to probe its limits, not to guarantee its predictive success.","The 'rationality' of the choice lies in the severity of the test it enables, not in the likelihood of the test being passed."]},"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's own terms without smuggling in induction, provided the preference is interpreted as a methodological rule for selecting the most severe test-object rather than an inductive bet on future truth. The cost of this defense is the abandonment of any claim that acting on the best-corroborated theory is 'rational' in the sense of maximizing expected utility or probability of success; it is rational only in the sense of being the most critical stance available.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If 'acting on a theory' logically entails assuming its future reliability proportional to past success, then the preference smuggles in induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the scientist cannot distinguish between 'choosing the best test candidate' and 'choosing the most likely true guide for action,' the defense collapses.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If Popper's own practical advice implies a hidden probabilistic assumption about the uniformity of nature, the distinction is merely verbal.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Reframe the scientist's 'preference' not as a prediction of future performance (which would require induction) but as a commitment to subject the boldiest, most informative conjecture to the next round of falsification. Since corroboration reports past severity of testing, preferring the highly corroborated theory means preferring the theory that has survived the hardest attempts to kill it, thereby offering the best chance for future learning (falsification), not the best chance for future confirmation.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
